title: Antarctic meltwater alters future projections of climate and sea level

paper_content.abstract: Imperfect understanding of ice sheet-climate interactions poses challenges for projecting the impacts of ice sheet mass loss on future climate and sea level. Here we couple a dynamic Antarctic ice sheet model and global climate model to simulate ice sheet-climate interactions. In our single-model, single-member modeling framework, we find sea level and climate projections are significantly modified from uncoupled simulations neglecting Antarctic meltwater under RCP8.5 and RCP4.5. Antarctic meltwater yields surface air temperatures up to 1.5°C higher in parts of the Northern Hemisphere, while broadly dampening temperature rise in the Southern Hemisphere. Due to radiative feedback changes, both emissions scenarios have global mean surface temperature warming ~0.3°C lower in the coupled scenario than the control by 2100, with a maximum anomaly of ~1°C at 2200 under RCP8.5. This slows Antarctica’s contribution to global mean sea level rise. Total Antarctic sea level contributions under RCP8.5 (2100: ~0.3 m, 2200: >3 m) include substantial contributions from East Antarctica, though not under RCP4.5 (2100: ~0.1 m, 2200: >1 m). Regionally, projected sea level is up to 0.9 m higher in the Pacific than the global mean Antarctic contribution under RCP8.5 at 2200.
paper_content.introduction:
The climate system is undergoing unprecedented changes as atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations continue to rise1. The resulting energy imbalance has accelerated ice sheet mass loss and sea level rise, which are projected to continue in coming centuries2. Current pledges submitted by parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change are insufficient for meeting the Paris Agreement’s Long-Term Temperature Goal of limiting global mean surface temperature (GMST) rise to “well below” 2°C above pre-industrial values while “pursuing efforts” to limit it to 1.5°C3. These pledges imply a 2.4-2.6°C GMST rise by 2100, while current policies imply 2.7°C warming4,5. Insufficient global mitigation risks are locking in large-scale ice sheet mass loss, exposing people and ecosystems around the world to substantial sea level rise. By 2060, over one billion people could be living in low elevation (<10 m above sea level) coastal areas, increasing the risks of sea level rise impacts for socially and geographically vulnerable populations6,7. Understanding interactions between ice sheets and the broader climate system will be key to constraining future Antarctic ice sheet (AIS) stability, global climate, and sea level8,9 which in turn has implications for global policy and climate justice10.

Observations confirm that the AIS increasingly contributed to global mean sea level rise (GMSLR) in recent decades11, while model projections suggest that the AIS could become the dominant contributor to GMSLR in the coming centuries2. Incursions of Antarctic circumpolar deep water in ice shelf cavities have been implicated as a cause of recent mass loss and grounding line retreat in sectors of East Antarctica12. Surface melt is currently observed to various extents across many ice shelves13 and is expected to become more frequent and longer lasting under medium to high emissions scenarios14. Additionally, continued atmospheric warming increases the potential for meltwater-driven hydrofracturing15, with ice shelves which provide substantial buttressing, being especially vulnerable16.

As the AIS loses mass, meltwater and solid ice enter the Southern Ocean. The current generation of global climate models participating in phases 5 and 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP5 and CMIP6, respectively) lack interactive marine-based ice sheets capable of simulating dynamic ice sheet evolution, such as grounding line retreat, while iteratively coevolving with other climate model components17. As a result, CMIP5-6 simulations underestimate ice sheet melt responses under increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, and the impact of meltwater discharge on future climate and sea level17–19. In turn, meltwater-induced climate responses impact ice sheet evolution and consequently the timing and magnitude of future GMSLR. The locations of ice sheet mass loss determine the spatial distribution of sea level responses around the world, emphasizing the need to consider gravitational, rotational, and Earth deformation effects on sea level10,20,21 in addition to climate-ice sheet interactions.

To assess climatic responses to greenhouse gas forcing and AIS discharge, prior modeling studies have conducted freshwater forcing experiments by adding meltwater to the Southern Ocean22–26. Despite variations in the location, quantity, and timing of freshwater input in these studies, modeled responses have several commonalities, including expanded Southern Ocean sea-ice, delayed GMST rise, increased ocean stratification, and subsurface ocean warming around the Antarctic margin. Warmer subsurface ocean temperatures and slowed atmospheric warming impact ice sheet evolution through increased basal melt and delayed surface melt, respectively. To better understand these interactions and more far-field impacts of Antarctic meltwater on the global climate system, dynamic ice sheets should be interactively embedded within global climate models27 and efforts to achieve this are advancing28. Recently, numerical experiments using coupling schemes under climate change projection scenarios have been used to assess climate-ice sheet feedbacks29,30 and a Southern Ocean meltwater forcing intercomparison project is underway17.

Here, we present results from numerical simulations in which coupling is implemented between the Community Earth System Model (CESM) 1.2, a coupled global climate model which includes interactive atmosphere, ocean, land, and sea-ice modules31, and the Penn State University ice sheet model (PSU3D), a dynamic-thermodynamic ice sheet model32–34; (See Methods). We then use a global sea level model that includes 3D viscosity structure35,36 to understand the spatially variable sea level response resulting from Antarctic mass loss in our coupled ice sheet-climate simulations. Our coupling setup exchanges liquid and solid ice sheet discharge from PSU3D to coastal surface level grid cells in CESM, and passes 2m air temperature, 400m ocean temperature, and precipitation fields from CESM back to PSU3D. CESM does not simulate cavity circulation under floating ice shelves so bias-corrected ocean temperatures from CESM are extrapolated under ice shelves in PSU3D. Latent heat from solid ice discharge in PSU3D is accounted for in CESM. Latent heat from liquid melt is accounted for in PSU3D and therefore not reflected in modeled ocean temperatures in CESM. Ice sheet topography in CESM is fixed, while changes in topography evolve in PSU3D. As a result, changes in ice sheet surface height and extent simulated in PSU3D are not felt by the CESM atmosphere or land surface model. Temperature and precipitation values received by PSU3D are lapse rate corrected and surface melt is calculated with a positive degree day scheme, accounting for the partial refreezing of meltwater in the firn layer. Marine ice cliff instability (MICI) dynamics are included (See Methods), providing substantially more meltwater forcing than most previous climate-ice sheet studies. While the validity of MICI remains contested37, the intent here is to explore the global impact of meltwater forcing while including brittle ice dynamics which have informed high-end sea level projections.

We explore changes in climate and sea level under future emissions scenarios RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 from 2005 to 2215. RCP scenarios were used rather than SSPs to make the best use of prior model simulations. RCP4.5 approximately corresponds to SSP2-4.5 and RCP8.5 to SSP5-8.538. While global mitigation efforts should preclude the RCP8.5 scenario in the long-term, we include this scenario because it tracks historical CO2 emissions39 and provides a useful case study for understanding coupled modeling responses. We include RCP4.5 as it results in end-of-century temperatures that are around or slightly above 2°C40. Within the text, ‘coupled’ refers to the simulations with interactive coupling between the ice sheet model and climate model and ‘control’ (or ‘uncoupled’) refer to the simulations with no interactive AIS which are equivalent to a standard CESM1.2 simulation, which produces minimal meltwater41. Due to computational constraints, simulations have one ensemble member per emissions scenario. There is no interactive Greenland Ice Sheet in any simulations presented here as we focus on the Antarctic response. This work builds upon the one-way coupled modeling protocol of Sadai et al. (2020) by implementing interactive coupling.
paper_content.results:
Antarctic contribution to global mean sea level rise
In agreement with modern observations (See Methods), we find that from 2005-2020 the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) contributes to a sea level rise while the East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS) displays a slight mass gain (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1). Under RCP8.5, the EAIS begins consistently contributing to sea level rise by 2030, and by 2040 under RCP4.5. Under RCP8.5, the EAIS mass loss increases mainly due to ice shelf melting under a warming atmosphere, leading to an increase in iceberg calving and ice cliff failure at marine-terminating ice margins. As a result, the GMSLR contribution from the EAIS surpasses that from the WAIS by 2080 (Supplementary Table 1). By 2100, cumulative GMSLR contributions from West and East Antarctica are similar: 0.15 m from WAIS and 0.19 m from EAIS, producing a total contribution of 0.34 m (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Table 1). This is on the upper end of the 0.03–0.34 m range projected for Antarctica in IPCC AR6 under RCP8.52 and consistent with uncoupled climate-ocean-ice sheet simulations that also included ice cliff calving processes34. The WAIS contribution by 2100 is dominated by Thwaites Glacier retreating on reverse-sloped bedrock (i.e., from Marine Ice Sheet Instability, MISI, driven retreat) (Fig. 1c). Both Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers are mostly lost in the RCP8.5 simulation by the mid-22nd century. By 2200, both the Ross and Filchner-Ronne ice shelves collapse, the EAIS margin undergoes widespread mass loss, the Antarctic peninsula thins, and the WAIS retreats (Fig. 1d). Despite the onset of MISI in West Antarctica, the EAIS remains the dominant contributor to GMSLR through the end of the RCP8.5 simulation. The total GMSLR contribution from Antarctica by 2200 is 3.37 m, of which 1.75 m is sourced from the EAIS and 1.62 m from the WAIS (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Table 1).

Under RCP4.5, lower greenhouse gas forcing limits the AIS GMSLR contribution to 0.13 m by 2100 with 0.1 m from WAIS and 0.03 m from EAIS (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Table 1). The pattern of ice loss mirrors that of RCP8.5 with Thwaites Glacier retreating and Ronne-Filchner thinning, but ice shelf thinning is less extensive overall, particularly in the EAIS (Fig. 1a). By 2200 the AIS GMSLR contribution reaches 1.17 m with 0.97 m from WAIS and 0.2 m from EAIS (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Table 1). The long-term view shows the impact of reducing greenhouse gas forcing; while WAIS still retreats substantially, large sections of the EAIS and portions of the Antarctic peninsula remain intact under RCP4.5 thereby limiting the AIS contribution to GMSLR.

Polar climate response
As CESM has static ice sheet topography, while PSU3D has evolving ice sheet topography, air temperatures noted here represent advected changes from evolving ocean conditions and do not reflect changes in the local land surface within CESM. In our coupled RCP8.5 experiment, surface air temperature (SAT) increases ~2–4°C by 2100 across the Southern Ocean and AIS (Fig. 2a). Regionally, this is ~1–4°C cooler than the uncoupled simulation (Fig. 2b). By the end of the 22nd century, there is widespread 5–10°C warming across the ice sheet, especially in the Ross and Weddell Sea regions, although this is up to ~7°C cooler than the uncoupled control simulation across the coastal region (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). Under RCP4.5, SAT increases by ~1-2°C by 2100 in the coupled simulation, except in the region of the Ross Sea where temperatures are lower by the end of 2100 and 2200 as compared to the start of the simulation (Supplementary Figs. 3a, 4a). Compared to the uncoupled simulation, SAT is ~1°C cooler by 2100, although the coupled simulation is slightly warmer in a few locations (Supplementary Fig. 3b). By 2200 the cooler temperatures in the coupled simulation as compared to the control are more pronounced with the largest difference in the Ross Sea (Supplementary Fig. 4b).

Throughout the RCP8.5 simulation, precipitation over the Southern Ocean increases (Fig. 2c; Supplementary Fig. 2c), although this change is less than in the uncoupled simulation (Fig. 2d; Supplementary Fig. 2d). The same overall patterns are found in RCP4.5 except the coupled simulation has slightly more precipitation than the control around Queen Maud and Wilkes Land by 2100 (Supplementary Fig. 3c, d). By 2200, precipitation in the coupled simulation has increased (Supplementary Fig. 4c) but is consistently lower in the RCP4.5 coupled simulation compared to the control (Supplementary Fig. 4d).

By 2100, under RCP8.5, ocean temperatures at 400 m depth warm substantially across the Southern Ocean (Fig. 2e), driven by freshwater-induced stratification and reduced vertical mixing. The greatest warming is in the Weddell Sea, with a 3°C temperature rise compared to the start of the simulation; the Ross Sea and EAIS margin near Wilkes Land warm by ~1°C. The end of century difference between the coupled and control simulations (Fig. 2f), as compared to the warming over time in the coupled simulation (Fig. 2e), shows that much of the warming is due to meltwater forcing. By 2200, 400 m ocean temperatures show widespread ~2°C warming relative to the start of the simulation (Supplementary Fig. 2e), with the Ross Sea ~4°C warmer in the coupled simulation than the control (Supplementary Fig. 2f). Under RCP4.5, the Weddell Sea and region around Wilkes Land are 3°C and 1°C warmer, respectively, by 2100 (Supplementary Fig. 3e). As in RCP8.5, much of this warming is due to the impact of meltwater (Supplementary Fig. 3f). By 2200 in RCP4.5, warming intensifies with ~2°C warming across the Southern Ocean since the start of the simulation (Supplementary Fig. 4e) and temperatures in the Ross and Weddell Seas up to 4°C higher in the coupled simulation than the control (Supplementary Fig. 4f).

The impacts of these climatic changes on the ice sheet explain the mass loss and contribution to GMSLR. Increases in SAT drive surface melt and induce hydrofracturing and ice shelf thinning while the accumulated ocean heat (i.e., warming at 400 m) increases basal melt under buttressing ice shelves. The concentration of heat in the Ross and Weddell Seas flips cold ice-shelf cavity circulation to warm cavity circulation patterns, accelerating loss of the large ice shelves, triggering MISI and in some places, ice cliff calving.

Global climate response
Our coupled simulations show that the impacts of AIS discharge into the Southern Ocean are felt globally (Fig. 3). In both RCP4.5 and RCP8.5, freshwater forcing begins suppressing greenhouse gas induced GMST rise by the middle of the 21st century (Fig. 3c). Under RCP8.5, GMST is 0.33°C lower by 2100 and 1.05°C lower by 2200 in the coupled simulation than in the control (Fig. 3d; Table 1). Under RCP4.5, GMST in the coupled simulation is 0.29°C lower by 2100 and 0.31°C lower by 2200 than in the control (Fig. 3d, Table 1). Compared to prior uncoupled experiments with the same models26, the impact of Antarctic meltwater on GMST is reduced due to the delayed ice sheet mass loss, and, therefore, lower meltwater input, that results from the interactive coupling.

The delayed GMST warming resulting from Southern Ocean freshwater forcing in our coupled simulations is caused by both a stronger ocean heat uptake efficiency (i.e., more efficient heat storage in the subsurface ocean) and a stronger atmospheric radiative feedback (i.e., more efficient radiative damping at the top of the atmosphere) (ref. 42; See Methods). The former is owing to the increased ocean stratification and vertical heat redistribution in the Southern Ocean manifested as subsurface warming (Fig. 2f). The latter is due to the broad surface cooling in both the Southern Ocean and the tropical Pacific driven by freshwater forcing and large-scale teleconnections (Supplementary Fig. 6)42–44. The Southern Ocean cooling anomalies and sea-ice expansion locally enhance surface albedo feedback, whereas the tropical East Pacific surface cooling drives a more-stabilizing cloud feedback and lapse-rate feedback, resulting from the strengthened tropical west-east zonal sea surface temperature gradient45,46. The net radiative feedback parameter over the 21st century is therefore strengthened from −1.02 W/m²/K to −1.13 W/m²/K in the coupled RCP8.5 simulation, corresponding to a 0.4°C decrease in effective climate sensitivity (from 3.8°C to 3.4°C) relative to the uncoupled control simulation. The results are qualitatively consistent with the findings in our prior uncoupled freshwater forcing simulations26,42.

Although GMST increases at a slower rate compared to our control simulations, the coupled simulations exhibit strong regional SAT variations (Fig. 3a, b). For example, by 2100 in RCP8.5, surface air temperatures over the Southern Ocean are ~1–1.5°C cooler, central and east Asia and the North Pacific are 0.3°C warmer, and the North Atlantic, including Greenland, eastern North America and western Europe are 1-2°C warmer than in the uncoupled simulation (Fig. 3a). By 2200 in RCP8.5 (Supplementary Fig. 5a), anomalous cooling over the Southern Ocean continues, with temperatures >3°C cooler in the coupled experiment near the Antarctic continent. By 2100 under RCP4.5 the difference between the coupled and control experiments shows a bipolar temperature pattern with anomalous cooling in the Southern Hemisphere and anomalous warming in the Northern Hemisphere but the pattern differs from that seen in RCP8.5 with no strong warming over the North Atlantic and instead more diffuse warming across Asia, North Africa, and the Pacific Ocean (Fig. 3b). By 2200 in RCP4.5, anomalous cooling of ~1°C occurs over the Southern Ocean and Arctic with slight warming across much of the Northern Hemisphere and the most pronounced warming of ~0.5°C along the Pacific coast of North America (Supplementary Fig. 5c).

The higher temperatures in the North Atlantic and North Pacific point to the existence of a bipolar seesaw, a pattern previously identified in Southern Ocean freshwater forcing experiments43,47,48. In RCP8.5, future slowing of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), defined as the maximum overturning at 24-26°N, is found to be largely delayed (Fig. 4a). In the coupled RCP8.5 simulation, the AMOC remains stronger than in the control from 2075 until the end of the simulation. The maximum difference between AMOC strength in the two simulations occurs at 2100 when the strongest signal of enhanced warming in both air (Fig. 3b) and sea surface temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 6) is observed in the coupled simulation. In RCP4.5, both the coupled and control simulations exhibit initial AMOC weakening followed by a partial recovery beginning after 2125. Under RCP4.5 whether the coupled or control simulation shows stronger AMOC strength is variable over time (Fig. 4a). In addition, northward heat transport is found to decrease under both RCP8.5 and RCP4.5 forcing (Fig. 4b). The largest differences occur at low-to-mid northern latitudes where the Atlantic Ocean is most effective at transporting heat northward.

Coupled meltwater simulations under both RCP8.5 and RCP4.5 show a robust northward shift of the intertropical convergence zone, due to zonal-mean energetic constraints associated with the anomalous inter-hemispheric surface temperature gradient49. In the Southern Hemisphere, wide-spread surface cooling is accompanied with broad drying while in the Northern Hemisphere, precipitation generally increases (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 5), which may arise from both local temperature changes or remote tropical teleconnections50. Under RCP8.5, zonal mean precipitation in the control simulation changes little over time (Fig. 3g) while in the coupled simulation it enhances north of the equator and diminishes to the south (Fig. 3h).

Broader Implications of Antarctic Ice Loss
Antarctic mass loss has important implications for people around the world. Fully understanding the potential impact of Antarctica’s contribution to sea level necessitates analyzing the spatial pattern of the sea level response. Global sea level change patterns from ice sheet mass loss are spatially variable due to gravitational, rotational, and Earth deformational (GRD) effects51. Using a 3D viscoelastic Earth structure model (See Methods) which includes anomalously low viscosities under the WAIS allows us to account for the sea level impact of water expulsion into the open ocean from formerly ice-covered areas undergoing uplift due to glacial isostatic adjustment52. Patterns of sea level change from GRD effects vary spatially and temporally depending on the regions of Antarctic mass loss21,51. Consistent with prior research10,21 we find that regions northward of 30°S will experience sea level rise higher than the Antarctic contribution to GMSLR regardless of emissions scenario and timescales. However, the most heavily impacted regions vary (Fig. 5). Under RCP4.5 by 2100 the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic Ocean basins, including the Caribbean, experience 0.03 m higher regional sea level rise than the global mean (Fig. 5a). By 2200 the pattern is similar but the difference between the highest impacted regions increases by an order of magnitude to 0.3 m (Fig. 5c). Under RCP8.5 by 2100, most of the Pacific basin is projected to experience regional sea level rise of up to 0.09 m higher than the GMSLR of 0.34 m (Fig. 5b). This pattern remains at 2200 with areas in the central Pacific experiencing 0.9 m more regional sea level rise than the GMSLR of 3.37 m while the Indian and Atlantic Ocean basins experience 0.6 and 0.7 m higher regional sea levels, respectively (Fig. 5d). These regional changes are solely based on the Antarctic response but realized sea level would also depend on Greenland mass loss, thermosteric responses, and other factors which are not accounted for here21,53.

Contrasting the global sea level response to the influence of meltwater on GMST has implications for global mitigation efforts and climate (in)justice10. Under RCP8.5, the timing when GMST exceeds 1.5–2°C above preindustrial (defined here following IPCC AR6 as when the 20-year rolling mean exceeds 1.5–2°C above the 1850–1900 average) is minimally affected by the meltwater induced delay in GMST rise (Supplementary Fig. 7a). This is because these warming values are surpassed before the meltwater-induced delayed warming effect strengthens. In our simulations, under high emissions (RCP8.5) 1.5°C is passed by 2026 and 2°C is delayed by 1 year in the coupled simulation. Under RCP4.5, 1.5°C and 2°C are each delayed by 1 year in the coupled simulation (Supplementary Fig. 7b). Given that these are single model runs with one set of models, how meltwater effects and other climate feedbacks impact the timing of different temperature thresholds remains deeply uncertain.

While the timing of the Long-Term Temperature Goal is minimally impacted, the long-term difference in GMST when accounting for meltwater input and feedbacks is substantial (Table 1) and relevant for informing future global mitigation target setting. The strength of the delayed GMST warming that occurs from Antarctic meltwater forcing should be considered alongside other climate feedbacks, such as the anticipated enhanced warming effect of permafrost melt. The combined impacts of climatic changes that influence GMST with other impacts such as sea level rise could pose substantial challenges if a GMST-based metric was used to inform international policy post-210010. In this study we find that GMST is 1.05°C lower under RCP8.5 by 2200 in the coupled simulation compared to the control, but this relatively cooler climate trajectory is commensurate with an Antarctic GMSLR contribution of 3.37 m and regional sea level rise of up to 4.3 m in the Pacific (Fig. 5d). Under RCP4.5, GMST is 0.31°C lower in the coupled simulation by 2200 while Antarctica’s contribution to GMSLR is 1.17 m and regional sea level rise of up to 1.5 m occurs in the Pacific and Indian Ocean basins and Caribbean Sea (Fig. 5c). In other words, while the loss of ice sheet mass results in a slightly lower GMST rise in the coupled simulations, it drives substantial sea level rise. This supports previous work which has argued that focusing on GMST as a metric to inform climate action could exacerbate climate justice concerns10. Even with a slower rate of warming, any continued increase in sea level poses risks to island and coastal communities, and raises wide-ranging issues of intergenerational inequity and distributive injustice10. The implications for justice and policy are complex and influenced by many other factors that require further detailed study.
paper_content.methods:
Model descriptions and initialization
The climate model used is Community Earth System Model 1.2.2 with Community Atmospheric Model 5 atmospheric physics (CESM1-CAM5)31. CESM1.2 is a coupled global Earth system model containing interactive ocean, atmosphere, sea-ice, and land models linked via a coupler. The continent and ocean boundaries do not change in CESM1.2. CESM1.2 does not include fully interactive Greenland or Antarctic ice sheets58. It was run with 1° resolution for the ocean and sea-ice components and 0.9×1.25° resolution for the atmosphere and land components. The model grid has a displaced pole over Greenland. It is initialized with 20th century restart files. Simulations spanning the period from 2005-2200 and were conducted under Representative Concentration Pathway RCP8.5 and RCP4.559.

The Antarctic ice sheet model used is the Penn State University ice sheet model (PSU3D)32,33. PSU3D is a three-dimensional ice sheet model that approximates ice flow using hybrid ice dynamics with an imposed parameterization of ice flux across the grounding line60, allowing for realistic simulation of grounding line retreat32. In these simulations it is run at a 10 km resolution with basal sliding coefficients obtained from an inverse run matching modeled surface elevations and observations61. Initial conditions were from DeConto et al. 34, which included simulations using offline CESM1.2 forcing. Bed topographic boundary conditions use Bedmap262. We use CESM1.2 and PSU3D with Bedmap2 boundary conditions to make the best use of previously run control experiments.

Models were run on the NCAR Cheyenne high performance computing system63. For the control scenarios, there is no freshwater forcing provided by the PSU3D ice sheet model. Testing determined that our RCP8.5 control matched the SAT evolution of the standard CMIP5 CESM1 simulation for RCP8.5, which is used for the time series in Fig. 364. For RCP4.5, data from CESM1-CAM5_rcp45_r1i1p1 obtained from the CMIP5 data repository was used as a control65. Preindustrial temperature data was obtained from the CMIP5 data repository66.

Coupling methodology
CESM1.2 and PSU3D are run with an annual interactive coupling scheme allowing for a dynamic response of the ice sheet to changes in the climate model, and response of the climate system to ice sheet freshwater discharge. The annual coupling is accomplished as follows67. An initial climatology is used to force PSU3D for one model year (2005), provided from a standard CESM1.2 control simulation lacking additional meltwater forcing. The ice sheet model is then run for one model year to provide liquid water and solid ice discharge from the ice sheet, interpolated onto the CESM1.2 ocean grid at the nearest coastal ocean cell from where the mass loss occurs in the ice sheet. Latent heat is accounted for as solid ice melts. The ice sheet model internally determines which types of ice sheet discharge exit as a solid or liquid. Latent heat of the solid ice discharge phase change is accounted for in the climate model while latent heat for liquid fields is accounted for within the ice sheet model32. Latent heat from fields the ice sheet counts as liquid is accounted for within the ice sheet model. This may underestimate the delayed warming effect of ice sheet discharge on global climate; therefore, the extent of the delayed warming effect seen in this study should be taken as a lower bound. The fields the ice sheet model outputs as liquid melt components include ice sheet basal melt, sub-ocean ice face melt, percolation of meltwater to the base, and the counter effect of basal refreezing while the solid ice discharge forcing contains ice lost from calving and cliff failure. Liquid and solid discharge components enter the climate model at the surface ocean level55,68. While injecting freshwater at depth can lead to more mixing and a deeper mixed layer and work with other ocean models has shown the depth of freshwater input to have an effect in other models69, previous work with CESM indicates that there is little difference in CESM1-simulated ocean surface temperature, salinity, and sea-ice responses when freshwater is applied at depth versus in experiments where freshwater is added at the surface41. Following the calculation of interpolated liquid and solid ice sheet discharge, CESM1.2 is then run for one model year to obtain a meltwater-perturbed climatology. Ocean temperature at 400 m depth, 2 m surface air temperatures, and precipitation are then passed back to the ice sheet. The ice sheet model is built to intake ocean temperatures at 400 m as this depth level is representative of where warm deep water enters the Amundsen Sea Embayment70,71.

Initial surface topography is provided to the climate sheet model by the ice sheet model at the first timestep. At subsequent timesteps, deviations between the input topography and evolving ice sheet topography are accommodated via lapse rate corrections for temperature and precipitation70. The fraction of input precipitation that falls as snow versus rain is parameterized based on the input surface air temperature. The ice sheet model surface mass balance calculations account for surface melting and refreezing as well as percolation of liquid water below the ice sheet surface layer. Surface melt is calculated via a positive degree day scheme, which calculates melt from the input temperature and precipitation, with melt beginning at -1°C based on observational relationships72.

Ocean forcing of the ice sheet
The ocean melt rate parameterization is a quadratic function of the temperature difference between the nearest ocean grid cell and the depth-dependent freezing temperature which is defined as follows.

Ocean melt = (K T ρw c W ) / (L f ρi) |T o − T f | (T o − T f ) (1)

Where T o is input 400 m ocean temperature, T f is the freezing-point temperature at the base of the ice at a given depth, ρ w and ρ i are the densities of water and ice, c W is the specific heat of ocean water, L f is the latent heat of fusion, K T is a transfer factor, and K is a set of tunable parameters32.

This parameterization has been shown to be one of the best performing options for representing both integrated shelf melt and grounding line melt73. Melting at submerged vertical ice faces is calculated from the ocean melt rate of surrounding grid cells and increased by a scaling factor of 2 to better match observations. This scaling factor is lower than the scaling factor of 10 which was used in previous uncoupled ice sheet simulations34,70.

To bring the ocean temperatures being passed to the ice sheet into closer agreement with observational values, the ocean temperature at 400 m is bias corrected using World Ocean Atlas 2018 observational temperatures74,75. As CESM1.2 does not have ocean cavities under ice shelves, ocean temperatures are taken from the static edge of the continent using a grid-cell-by-grid-cell stepping approach to determine the ocean temperature at the ice shelf edge wherever it is available in the ocean model. The ice sheet model interpolates them to the ice sheet grid and linearly extrapolates a value back into the interior of the shelf. To avoid a small number of warm grid cells from having an oversized impact on melt rates when interpolated over a large shelf, a single value is calculated as the average of all ocean grid cells in polygons specifying each ice shelf’s area and that one value is interpolated under that shelf. To bring melt rates in the Amundsen Sea region into closer alignment with observational values, a 2.5°C anomaly is added in that region, similar to the bias corrections applied in previous work with PSU3D34,70.

Calving sensitivity and cliff failure
As in previous work with PSU3D, surface crevasse depth is influenced by surface melt and rainwater, assuming a quadratic relationship between meltwater production (R) and crevasse penetration depth (d w).

d w = CALVLIQ R 2 (2)

This meltwater enhanced crevassing (d w) influences ice shelf hydrofracturing and calving33,34. To bring mass loss from calving in line with observations over the modern period the CALVLIQ parameter is set to 35 m-1 yr2.

As used here, the ice sheet model accounts for enhanced calving at thick (O 1000 m) marine-terminating ice fronts that have lost their buttressing ice shelves, leaving tall subaerial ice cliffs prone to brittle failure76. Ice cliff calving occurs at calving fronts where the stresses exceed the yield strength. The cliff calving parameterization is applied as a horizontal wastage with a maximum rate of 7.7e3 m/y34. We note that the role of marine ice cliff calving in future Antarctic ice loss remains contested37,77, with much of the uncertainty caused by a lack of observations and poorly constrained physical properties of damaged glacial ice78,79.

Model validation
Before the coupled run was integrated, several shorter tests were done under transient climate forcing from 2005-2020 to check for consistency between model results and existing observational measurements. The total modeled rate of basal melt around the continent from 2005-2017 is 1343.21 Gt/yr67, in alignment with rates from 80 [1280-1628 Gt/yr] and 81 [1010-1310 Gt/yr]. The total modeled calving rate over this period is 974.874 Gt/yr67, slightly below the estimate of 1177-1465 Gt/yr in ref. 80. The modeled basal melt rates at the Pine Island, Thwaites, Ross, and Ronne-Filchner ice shelves are 36.4, 35.1, 0.28, and 0.27 m/yr, respectively67 as compared to 81 [14, 26.7, 0.3, 0.2 m/yr] and 82 [16.2, 17.2, 0.3, 0.3 m/yr]. While modeled rates of ice loss are higher than the average observed melt rates at PIG and Thwaites, the total sea level rise contribution from the WAIS is in line with observations and areas of higher melt rates (up to 43 m/yr) have been seen at the Thwaites grounding line83. From 2005 to 2017, the total modeled AIS sea level rise contribution is 2 mm, lower than the 7.4 ± 1.5 mm Antarctic contribution reported for 1992–202011 implying that the coupled simulation is slightly underestimating sea level rise contributions during this observational period. The spatial patterns of changes in ice thickness from 2005 to 2020 compare well with observations from 84 (their Fig. 1 compared to our Supplementary Fig. 1).

Sea level rise calculations
Global mean sea level contributions are calculated using the modified volume above flotation (VAF) method which accounts for the rise or fall of bedrock elevation below grounded ice which changes VAF but does not alter sea level85.

Geographically variable sea level changes accounting for gravitational, Earth rotational86 and Maxwell viscoelastic deformational87 effects are calculated by solving the sea level equation51,88. Calculations account for migrating shorelines and inundation of areas freed of marine grounded ice88,89. We adopt the finite volume sea level solver to solve the sea level equation on a global tetrahedral grid including 3D variations in Earth’s rheological structure35. We adopt the 3D viscosity structure and laterally varying lithospheric thickness model EM3D_L90 based on ANT-20 regional seismic tomography model91 in Antarctica and S362ANI global seismic tomography model92 across the rest of the globe. Lithosphere thickness in the model is based on 93 over Antarctica and a global model94 elsewhere. Globally, the adopted computational grid has an average spatial (lateral and radial) resolution of 12 km from the surface to the Mohorovičić Discontinuity (MOHO), 25 km to 220 km depth, and 50 km to the core mantle boundary. The grid is regionally refined in Antarctica, with a resolution of 6 km to the base of the MOHO, 12 km to 220 km depth, and 25 km to 350 km depth36. The ice sheet model provides the initial topography in Antarctica, and this is merged with ETOPO2 elsewhere.

Global energy budget analysis
The ocean heat uptake efficiency parameter (κ) and the radiative feedback parameter (λ) are calculated as:

κ = dN / dT, λ = d(N − F) / dT, (3)

Where dN is the global-mean net top of atmosphere radiation imbalance, dF is effective radiative forcing and dT is the global-mean near-surface air temperature change42. Based on the global-mean energy budget framework95,96, the transient global warming rate (dT/dt) can be approximated as:

dT/dt = (dF/dt) / (κ − λ) (4)

Where we substitute values of κ or λ from control or coupled simulations to isolate the impacts of ocean heat uptake efficiency or radiative feedback on the global warming rate42. Effective climate sensitivity is calculated as:

EffCS = −F 2x / λ (5)

Where F 2x represents the effective radiative forcing from a doubling of atmospheric carbon dioxide. The value of F 2x in CESM1.2 is 3.88 W m2 97. EffCS is an analog to equilibrium climate sensitivity except using λ from a transient state assuming λ remains constant until equilibrium42.

Data visualization
Spatial sea level maps were created in ArcGIS using a Goode homolosine ocean-oriented projection10,98. Figures 1–3 and supplemental figures were created with Cartopy99. Sea level maps use country outlines provided by Natural Earth shapefiles: Pacific groupings, 1:10m countries, 1:50m Tiny Country Points. On some figures scientific colormaps are from 100, 101.

Data availability
The climate data and spatial sea level mapping data generated in this study and referenced in the paper have been deposited in the University of Massachusetts Amherst ScholarWorks repository (https://doi.org/10.7275/6t64-wy56)102. The climate model data fields and spatial sea level data not referenced in this paper are available for non-commercial use from the corresponding authors due to difficulties hosting a large dataset externally. The ice sheet model data is available in the ScholarWorks repository (https://doi.org/10.7275/6t64-wy56)102. Data for the 1850-1900 baseline and CMIP5 RCP8.5 and RCP4.5 simulations are available from the Centre for Environmental Data Analysis64–66. Natural Earth country boundary data is available at www.naturalearthdata.com.

Code availability
CESM1.2 is available from the National Center for Atmospheric Research. The PSU3D code is available in the ScholarWorks repository102, please contact DP and RD for assistance running it. The 3D GIA model is available from the code’s developer Konstantin Latychev. Scripts for running the models and creating the figures are in the data repository (https://doi.org/10.7275/6t64-wy56).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Summary
--
Sadai et al. couple a older (CMIP5 era) version of the Community Earth System Model to a complex model of the Antarctic
ice sheet, and perform simulations of mid- and high-level climate change scenarios with and without the ice sheet coupling
enabled to show its impact on a number of regional and global climate metrics. Coupling of ice sheets into complex climate
models appropriate for CMIP-type projections is an important and emerging area of science and they demonstrate and
analyse a number of notable features that result from their coupling which are significant and worth publicising to a general
audience. The paper is clearly written, with appropriate figures and referencing. For me, the main weaknesses is the degree
to which the quantitative extent of some of their results - which follow from a simulation of Antarctic ice sheet mass loss that
is at the very top end of the IPCC-assessed range and a highly parameterized anomaly coupling method, with no attempt to
address any model uncertainty - is likely to be highly model dependent. This is not uncommon for this new area of research,
but I think the authors could help their readers by doing more to put the their ice sheet simulation in the context of other
studies and guard against readers seeing the numbers they put on their consequent global changes as "likely" features of
future climate change, rather than the illustrations of the potential of possible physical mechanisms in the climate system that
they are.
General Comments
--
As far as positive's go, my comments in the Summary pretty much say it all. This was an interesting and enjoyable paper to
read. The increased sophistication of the climate model, the detail in the physical analysis of impacts of ice sheet coupling in
the climate system and translation of the mean sea level changes to region patterns via global sea level modelling all make
this a significant step forward from previous Nature Communication publications on this topic (e.g Park et al 2023).
I think this is an important paper that highlights important, unappreciated potential global impacts of ice sheet coupling.
However, I think it's also important that the audience is aware of the relevant limitations (which are not uncommon for this
field) of the modelling system that produces the simulations, and that readers can consider the quantitative detail they're
being shown appropriately. That level of model description might not be what is usually considered appropriate for this
journal, but the approximations in their method and model are an important factor in the results they get and I think that
readers ought to have some awareness of the very broad physical approximations going on under the hood of the
interactively icy parts of the model, compared to what they perhaps expect from the explicit physics in other parts of a CMIP
climate model like CESM-CAM.
I am a little concerned this is lost by rather briefly summarising it all at the end; there is a just simple reference to a previous
paper for the ice sheet initialisation, no real sensitivity test on tuning the fundamental ocean coupling parameterisation in
their system, or the implications of the sizable, regionally-dependent anomaly adjustment that allows it to work with the
climate model biases. The surface coupling between the ice and CESM does not seem to be mentioned at all, and I do not
think it has been documented elsewhere? In terms of checking the performance of the coupled ice sheet/climate system the
first paragraph "Model Validation" section is welcome, but pretty much a broad-brush bare minimum of what I'd really want to
see in terms of having any real confidence in interpreting the results quantitatively. I realise Nat Comm is not a place that
welcomes that level of detail, hence my suggestion that a stronger caveat emptor be put on taking the numbers reported too
literally.
On top of the considerable uncertainty in the detail that arises from being unsure of the model formulation, the reponses
being analysed are probably at the outer edge of what is considered likely. The loss of mass from the ice sheet is at the top of the IPCC range, with a model that I think includes a somewhat controversial parameterisation of Marine Ice Cliff Instability, forced by a Scenario that is now considered an extreme at 2100 but they use extended to 2200. Their ocean coupling
mechanism is likely to further amplify the climate response - their parameterisation effectively immediately flushes cold melt
from the cavity and puts it in exactly the place where it will most increase stratification and exacerbate the sub-shelf warm
water that the melt calculation sees, guaranteeing a positive feedback. It's all physically possible, but far from the only set of
physically plausible responses. Since there is no uncertainty analysis presented it would be easy for resulting sea level rise
and GMST-mitigation numbers they report to be misinterpreted, rather than being seen as perhaps an upper plausible limit
on the possible Antarctic contribution.
A large degree of model dependence is an unavoidable fact in this emerging area of science. I hope that the authors are
involved in ongoing multi-model comparisons, like eg ISMIP7 (https://theghub.org/groups/ismip6/wiki) or MISOMIP2,
especially, considering their coupled abilities and ambitions to include an interactive GrIS, in coupled experiments of those
projects. Some coupled experiments were proposed in ISMIP6 (Nowicki et al. 2016 Geosci. Model Dev.), and it is likely that
more will be for CMIP7, with a focus, as here, on Antarctica.
Specific comments
--
lines 113,390,647: "fully coupled" is an ambiguous and usually inaccurate term for any model of the Earth System, including
this one. Many possible component couplings are simplistically parameterised or omitted entirely, and if "fully" is meant
simply to indicate that all the components that the modellers wanted to include are permitted to exchange information, it is
vague and subjective.
lines 120,646: I think an explicit comment on the non-use of the coupled Greenland ice sheet component of CESM would be
good. CESM has been a a pioneer of work with ice sheet coupling and is known for its interactive GrIS which you've actively
decided not to use here.
line 122: it might help orient readers to note that, if I read it right, this is an evolution of the same model and simulation
protocol used in Sadai et al. 2020, with the important difference that now the models are interactively coupled together.
line 123: it would be helpful to note how these older scenarios map onto more recent IPCC AR6 SSP framework - and
ideally onto the public thinking on the sorts of Scenarios that are now considered realistic and are being proposed for the
next round of climate projections (https://wcrp-cmip.org/scenariomip-cmip7-proposal). While it's not untrue to say that
RCP8.5 is policy-relevant to mid-century, it is very extreme after that. RCP8.5's most plausible use for me is as the "useful
case study for understanding coupled modeling responses" - and that's justification enough, but this is what should be
foregrounded, not the suggestion of policy relevance that risks subsequent results being misinterpreted.
line 139: Following cliff collapse, do the atmosphere, ocean and sea-ice models in CESM see a change in domain that
might change their boundary condition calculations for the ice sheet?
line 166: "melt-water induced suppression..." does this affect EAIS and WAIS equally? The implication that cooling
automatically implies a reduction loss from AIS ignores the significant response in AIS snowfall that many climate models
see with warming - in that case, for some timescales at least, cooling implies a milder increase in AIS snow and a net
increase in AIS mass loss. I'd like to see a little more of what happens on the surface in this model. Could the authors show
what the snow response in the RCPs in this model means for AIS VAF, the precipitation shown in figure 2c isn't enough to
see what's going on here.
Figure 3c, 3d, 4c: I didn't understand why the RCP4.5 lines only go to 2100 in these plots
line 307: Solving the global sea-level equation is a valuable addition to this paper, rather than just stopping with the global
mean sea level numbers. Does the change in solid earth eg WAIS uplift affect the ice sheet model as it runs, impact the
melting of WAIS as suggested by Gomez'15? Have mass change from Greenland or redistribution of ocean properties from
the climate model been included or just mass from AIS? If not, although it's fair to report these numbers as the influence of
AIS (possibly the dominant one?) on regional sea-level within what will be a wider picture that includes other influences, I'm
concerned that if this is just one component towards a very non-linear global picture the numbers reported in this part could
be misinterpreted.
line 333: The acronym LTTG is explained in passing very early on, and then only used, once, toward the very end of the
paper, by which time I'd forgotten what it meant. Could the full term be used here for clarity?
line 395: Although there's not a lot of coupled simulations of this sort for context, I think it would be helpful to include some
broader multi-model context of the AIS contribution to sea level, eg the standalone ISMIP6 AIS mass loss projections
(Seroussi et al. 2020). This would highlight the model dependency and very wide spread (both net positive and negative sea
level contributions are possible) of the state of knowledge in the community - adding interactive coupling to models does not
reduce that uncertainty and is not the reason (as far as I can tell) that Park23 and Siahaan22 get sea level contributions of
opposite signs.
line 660: ice sheet model initial conditions are really important in terms of determining the ice sheet behaviour over the
following century or two. I'd prefer more detail upfront than just a reference to go look elsewhere. In particular, in this context
of a coupled climate - ice sheet model are these ice initial conditions in equilibrium with some climate forcing from CESM?
Do they have an initial overall trend in VAF that is either baked into the initialisation or dependent on a systematic bias in
CESM boundary conditions that will give a signal regardless of the climate forcing or coupling they'll see in the future
simulations?
line 665: I'm a bit confused by the setup of the uncoupled control. Is this saying that the RCP8.5 control has no AIS fresh
water flux at all? Not even surface runoff, or mass from inventory capped snowpack that keeps ice sheet "in balance". Are
your experiments showing the impact of coupled water fluxes, or just of having some water coming from AIS at all.
Compared to what is said in Sadai et al. 2020 - I thought both experiment and control had flux, it's just that one was fixed and
the other varying?
line 692: This sort of coupling is not without precedent, but it is very simple and putting both liquid and solid fresh water into
the ocean at the surface, at the coastline, is likely to enhance the stratification effect and make the feedback to the melt
parameterisation stronger. Solid discharge and its latent heat requirements for melting would be spread and diluted over a
much wider area in reality and even if in CESM it makes no difference whether you put the coastal melt in at the surface or
depth as quoted, it's unrealistic either way - and the different approaches have. been shown to make a difference in other
models (Mathiot et al. Geosci. Model Dev. 2017) so this isn't really a justification that it really doesn't matter if the
parameterisation does this.
line 714: I think the use and tuning of the (somewhat controversial (Edwards et al 2019, Nature)) parameterisation of Marine
Ice Cliff Instability in PSU3D needs highlighting. I assume it is used here, since the main text talks about ice cliff failure, but it
does not appear in this model description. The fact that the significance of this aspect of model physics and how it should be
implemented in a model is debated in the community should should be perhaps be noted in the main text for a general
audience if it is playing a significant role in the result of the ice sheet simulation.
line 671: I would like some description of the surface coupling. I don't think this is mentioned at all, and I'm surprised this is
not more important in CESM's response to such large AIS warming. Is it based on how CESM deals with surface coupling to
Greenland or an external PDD scheme or some other downscaled mass/energy balance modelling? As already noted I
wanted to see more on what the model was doing with snow change component of the AIS VAF budget. My understanding
is that CESM (newer versions at least) have a very significant increase in snowfall, which would act to mitigate the discharge
or loss in the first century at least - this sort of result isn't apparent in your simulations and the precipitation in figure 2 is not
detailed enough to interpret in this way. Does the surface topography change in PSU3D affect the CESM topography - I
would assume so, and with ice thickness changes of many 100s of metres I imagine it would be important to the climate
model response, but I don't think this is explicitly mentioned anywhere? Do the atmosphere, ocean and sea-ice models in
CESM ever see a change in domain that might change their boundary condition calculations for the ice sheet, say after shelf
collapse?
line 692: This section describes a really important part of how your model is representing the interactions you are reporting
on and I felt it was passed over rather lightly. You mention that you use a (new?) scaling factor of 2, but the previously used
value, 5 times larger, reproduces observations better? Then despite this scaling, a general bias correction is used. And then,
an extra 3 degree correction is added for a particular key region. This all comes across as a bit arbitrary, and tuned to
reproduce a specific modern state - with this level of detail it's little difficult to trust when it's going to be used to assess the
sensitivity of the model to a change to a very different future state. When other cavities (eg Ross, Filchner) flip to warm ocean
conditions like current Amundsen, do they get the same extra 3 degrees in the coupling parameterisation too? Since you've
already corrected for ocean biases appropriate for the modern day regimes, does the 3 degree term need to be applied to all
warm water shelves, whenever and wherever they are seen?
line 731: PIG and Thwaites being relatively poor matches to obs is a bit worrying - they are small areas, so won't affect your
total WAIS contribution evaluation, but are crucial for the dynamic sensitivity of WAIS, which you then see as being less than
EAIS in the simulations.
line 749: 1.5cm at what date, or is that a constant offset?
line 742: Is the topographic information from the solid earth model coupled to anything, either
CESM or PSU3D?
line 787, 794: saying that data will be made available upon acceptance and that model code is available upon request -
neither allowing for peer review of this manuscript - is far from best practice in terms of open and reproducible science.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Summary / Key results
This paper presents results from coupled climate-Antarctic ice sheet model simulations under future emissions scenarios
RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 to evaluate the impact of feedbacks from ice-climate interactions. The outputs are then used to project
global sea level rise. The authors find that surface warming is delayed at 2100 compared to simulations where the ice sheet
is not coupled to the climate model. The contribution of the Antarctic Ice Sheet to global sea level rise is less than that in the
uncoupled simulation. Sea level rise is spatially uneven, with the Pacific experiencing a larger increase in mean sea level
than other regions.
Significance
This is an interesting study that shows a reduction in warming and subsequent melting of the Antarctic Ice Sheet when a
coupled ice sheet is included in future climate simulations. The most commonly cited future projections from CMIP5/6 do not
include meltwater or an interactive ice sheet; the authors here demonstrate that there are important interactions and
feedbacks that these experiments are neglecting and that need to be taken into account to obtain accurate projections.
I am not entirely convinced of the study’s novelty. I note that similar experiments have been done before (which the authors
cite): Park et al. (2023) and Siahaan et al. (2022). How is this work significantly different and/or how does it advance our
understanding? The authors should articulate this more clearly.
Validity/ Data and methodology/Analytical approach
The data analysis and interpretation is sound and the conclusions are justified. The authors have done a good job designing
the experiments so that the specific impacts of meltwater and the coupled ice sheet/climate can be isolated. However, I have
a few questions/concerns:
• The models are coupled on a relatively coarse timescale, as they only exchange information once every year. This could
be sufficient for ice sheet processes which react relatively slowly, but seasonal effects could be important for atmosphere,
ocean and sea ice.
• The climate model does not explicitly represent ice shelves, which limits the ability to infer basal melting rates underneath
the main ice shelves (Ross, Filchner-Ronne, etc).
• Melt from the Greenland Ice Sheet was not included in the simulation; this is okay for an Antarctic-focused study, but how
might the results change when Greenland is included? For example, I would expect the pattern of sea level rise to change
substantially with the reduction in solid ice mass in the Northern Hemisphere.
• The climate model used, CESM1.2, is relatively old (from the CMIP5 generation) and low-resolution when it comes to
atmosphere-ice-ocean interactions. For example, it does not represent coastal polynyas and Antarctic Bottom Water
formation correctly. How might this limit the conclusions?
Suggested improvements
• It would be helpful to comment on processes on sub-grid and sub-annual spatial/temporal scales and whether or not these
could be important.
• I would like a brief discussion of how the results might change if the impacts of melt from the Greenland Ice Sheet are
included (even if it is only in reference to other work)
Clarity and context
The paper is very clearly written and is placed in the appropriate context
References
References are appropriate
Your expertise: My expertise is mainly in climate and earth system modelling. I am less familiar with sea level and GIA
modelling and do not feel qualified to evaluate this portion of the manuscript.
Minor comments
Introduction
Line 73: over what time frame? More references?
Line 76: “various extents” is very vague. Surface melt in Antarctica is currently limited and not a significant contributor to
mass loss; how extensive is surface melt in terms of area, amount of freshwater? What regions are we talking about?
(Antarctic Peninsula yes; others?)
Line 80: which ice shelves are you referring to? Or is this just a general statement?
Line 122: “simulations” -> “simulation”
Lines 122-125: You justify the use of RCP 8.5 but not RCP 4.5—why this scenario?
Results
Line 139: The representation of ice cliff calving processes in models can be controversial, did you do any simulations where
you tested the sensitivity of the results to including this process?
Lines 163-168: Note that the effect of adding meltwater forcing is much bigger than the coupling effect.
Lines 182-183: temperature in the Ross Sea region is actually lower, this is very interesting! Why is that?
Lines 194-195: “By 2200 precipitation has increased and is consistently lower in the RCP4.5 coupled simulation …” this
doesn’t make sense, if precipitation increased it can’t be lower
Polar climate response section: what about sea ice coverage/extent? How important is that? How much do precipitation
changes contribute to surface mass balance changes over Antarctica?
Fig 3: Why does the RCP 4.5 simulation timeseries stop in 2100? I thought this was also run to 2200?
Lines 313-314: “regions northward of 30°S will experience sea level rise higher than the Antarctic contribution to GMSLR”:
this is confusing because it’s not as simple as saying Antarctica contributed x amounts of SLR in this location. It would be
better to give this number relative to global means.
Lines 330-331: “Given that these are single model runs with one set of models, policy implications are limited in the short
term.” This isn’t quite the right phrasing here and mixes several concepts. Yes, your study is limited to one model, and this
means there is substantial uncertainty in the numbers, but this is separate from the policy implications of the results.
Lines 343-346: “These combined impacts exacerbate climate justice concerns as SLR presents risks to recognition
justice for island and coastal communities, including the Alliance of Small Island States, and wide-ranging issues of
intergenerational inequity and distributive injustice” You’ve mentioned climate justice several times; acknowledging that this
is a serious issue, it’s not really the focus of this paper and seems like an odd thing to be emphasizing here in the results
Fig 5: nice figure!
Discussion
Lines 380-381: “Paleoclimate evidence shows signs of past ice sheet retreat in deep EAIS subglacial basins and while
future model projections show differing responses.” This sentence is grammatically incorrect, not sure how to interpret it
Lines 392-393: “An important next step will be the addition of an interactively coupled Greenland Ice Sheet model.” Yes, I
think this is very important and could affect the global patterns that you see. A bit more discussion of this aspect would be
helpful. What have others found when they coupled the GrIS?
Line 397: which intermediate complexity model? How much of an improvement is CESM 1.2?
Impact of ice shelf cavities not being explicitly represented? More discussion of study limitations is needed (annual time step
etc)
Methods:
Why do you show results for RCP 4.5 only to 2100? Text says you ran to 2200, if not please correct
Is a time step of one year really enough? Are there seasonal feedbacks that are not accounted for?
Ocean forcing of the ice sheet: is a bias correction based on present day values appropriate for future projections?
